analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to disclose their donors and closes loopholes letting foreign money into elections.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 193 Democratic cosponsors in the House, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would force corporations, unions, super PACs, and dark-money nonprofits to report election spending over $10,000 to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to reveal the people who fund them. Political ads would have to name their top funders on screen or on air. It would also tighten the ban on foreign money by covering paid online ads and ballot-measure campaigns, and make it a crime (up to five years in prison) to set up a company to hide a foreign national's election contribution. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for the political ads they see: the bill would put the top funders of campaign ads on screen, within 24 hours of spending. It would also benefit campaigns that operate openly, which would no longer compete against untraceable spending, and it would close paths by which foreign money can reach U.S. elections through shell companies and online ads.

how_it_helps.text: Organizations spending more than $10,000 on election-related activity would have to report it to the FEC within 24 hours, along with the identity of their beneficial owners and the major funders behind their spending.
Political ads would have to name their top funders on screen or in audio — the 'Stand By Every Ad' provision — so viewers can see who is paying for the message.

The ban on foreign money would extend to paid online and digital ads and to ballot initiative campaigns, and it would become a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to set up a shell company to hide a foreign national's election contribution.

For the first time, spending to influence federal judicial nominations would have to be disclosed, closing a gap where hundreds of millions of dollars in advertising for and against court nominees went unreported.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, dark-money nonprofits, super PACs, and trade groups that spend money to influence elections would bear new reporting duties within 24 hours of spending and would have to disclose their major funders in ads. Labor unions are covered too. Large online platforms would face new disclaimer and foreign-money rules for political ads. The public pays nothing directly, though more disclosed money could shift where and how groups advertise.

drawbacks.text: Organizations would have to file detailed reports within 24 hours of passing $10,000 in campaign spending, including the identities of their beneficial owners and major funders — a real compliance burden for small nonprofits and membership groups.

The bill's disclosure lists (the 'Top Five Funders' on ads) can expose the donors behind political speech, and critics of disclosure laws argue this can deter lawful participation in public debate; the bill itself includes an exception only for people facing serious threats, harassment, or reprisals.
The bill presumes the FEC can write and enforce the new rules; the commission is evenly split between the parties and frequently deadlocks, so even if enacted, implementation could stall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is voter knowledge: the largest funders behind political ads would be named on screen, and foreign-money loopholes closed with real penalties. The main costs fall on the groups spending the money: fast, detailed reporting within 24 hours, potential exposure of donors to public scrutiny (mitigated by a harassment exception in the bill text), and compliance burdens for nonprofits and membership groups. The bill relies on an evenly split FEC to write rules, which historically produces stalemates. On balance the transparency gains for voters are substantial and the burdens fall mainly on entities choosing to spend money to influence elections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House committees it was referred to without ever getting a markup or a vote, and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Cicilline introduced the DISCLOSE Act on February 21, 2023.
It attracted 193 cosponsors — 193 of 216 House Democrats — including the ranking members of the committees with jurisdiction.
It was referred to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary committees; the record shows no hearings, markups, or votes in any of them.
The only later action was a July 2023 change of first sponsor to Representative Pappas after Cicilline resigned from Congress, done by unanimous consent for administrative purposes.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend large undisclosed sums to influence elections kept operating without naming their funders.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 21, 2023 and recruited a large bloc of initial cosponsors; resigned from Congress in mid-2023, at which point Rep. Chris Pappas became first sponsor by unanimous consent.

for.name: 193 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of roughly nine in ten House Democrats.

for.name: Rep. Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Took over as first sponsor in July 2023 to keep the bill alive and continue adding cosponsors after Cicilline's resignation.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda after January 2023 and never scheduled the bill for consideration; the three committees of referral took no action on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 193 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans sponsored the bill, and with Republicans holding the House majority it never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: Their core business — spending large sums to influence elections and judicial nominations without naming funders — would become reportable within 24 hours, with top funders named in the ads themselves. This is the industry of influence the bill most directly targets.
Disclosure adds filing obligations and coordination restrictions, but groups willing to operate openly could continue spending; the rules mainly raise the cost of anonymity.

Platforms with 50 million or more U.S. users would face expanded foreign-money and disclaimer rules on political ads, but the compliance burden is modest relative to ad revenue and the bill exempts news publishers.
The bill extends the ban on foreign election spending to digital ads, ballot initiatives, and judicial-nomination campaigns, and criminalizes using shell companies to conceal foreign contributions.
